### Observed differences

- For six activities that draw on a common pool of resources (A01, A03, A13, A14, A17, A22), assignment work moved from one group of resources to another. In the earlier window the most used resource was User_104 with roughly 10–20 in 100 assignments (about 20 in 100 for A22), ahead of User_67 at about 8–13 in 100; in the later window User_104's share roughly halved (for A22 from about 20 to about 8 in 100), User_67 became the most used resource at about 13–18 in 100, and previously minor resources such as User_77 each took about 5–8 in 100. [ASSIGN001, ASSIGN002, ASSIGN004, ASSIGN005, ASSIGN006, ASSIGN007]
- Work also became more spread across resources: the combined share of everything outside the ten most used resources rose in the later window for all six activities, for example from about 38 to about 45 in 100 for A01 and from about 27 to about 34 in 100 for A22. [ASSIGN001, ASSIGN002, ASSIGN004, ASSIGN005, ASSIGN006, ASSIGN007]
- A07 shifted to a largely different set of resources: its three most used resources in the earlier window (about 10 in 100 assignments each) do not appear among the leading shares in the later window, which is led by a resource that previously held only about 4 in 100, together with several resources not previously prominent. [ASSIGN003]
- All seven resource profiles changed in the same "redistributed" direction, with dissimilarity of about 0.33–0.39 on the indicator's own scale, and each difference exceeds about 999 in 1000 random re-splits of the pooled data. [ASSIGN001, ASSIGN002, ASSIGN003, ASSIGN004, ASSIGN005, ASSIGN006, ASSIGN007]

### Inference

Support level: Supported hypothesis

The evidence supports the hypothesis that resource allocation changed for a set of activities. In the earlier window, assignments for A01, A03, A13, A14, A17 and A22 were concentrated on a group of resources led by User_104; in the later window that group's share fell sharply, User_67 became the most used resource, and a broader set of previously minor resources, including User_77, took a substantial share, with more work spread across the long tail. A07 was reallocated to a largely different set of resources altogether, its earlier leading resources no longer holding top shares. [ASSIGN001, ASSIGN002, ASSIGN003, ASSIGN004, ASSIGN005, ASSIGN006, ASSIGN007]

The screening found 7 resource items where about 0.005 would be expected if nothing had changed — far too many to attribute to chance as a whole — while control flow and timing produced no items (0 against about 0.17 and about 0.01 expected). All items agree in direction and in which groups of resources rose and fell, each difference exceeds about 999 in 1000 random re-splits, and every profile rests on roughly 120–280 assignment observations per window, so the shares are not based on a handful of cases. [ASSIGN001, ASSIGN002, ASSIGN003, ASSIGN004, ASSIGN005, ASSIGN006, ASSIGN007]

Limitations: the evidence shows only assignment shares per activity, so it cannot distinguish reassignment of the same cases from a changed mix of cases, and it cannot show why allocation moved. A13 and A14 have identical profiles, so they may reflect one shared allocation shift rather than two independent changes. The share of traces containing A07 also fell (about 82 to about 71 in 100), but with no participation item qualifying, this may be sampling variation. [ASSIGN003, ASSIGN004, ASSIGN005]

Other differences: none; the only qualified evidence concerns resource allocation. [ASSIGN001, ASSIGN002, ASSIGN003, ASSIGN004, ASSIGN005, ASSIGN006, ASSIGN007]
